items.caption: Factoring 360 down to primes
items.text: The factor tree splits 360 until every branch ends in a prime: 360 = 2 · 180 = 2 · 2 · 90, and so on, leaving the leaves 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5. Collected, that is 360 = 2³ · 3² · 5. A factor of 360 picks 0 to 3 twos, 0 to 2 threes and 0 or 1 five, so the exponents give the count directly: (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 24 factors.

items.caption: The ÷3 column: the multiples of 3 marked down the table
items.text: Reading down the highlighted column, every third number is marked as divisible by 3: those marks are the multiples 3, 6, 9, 12, … produced by multiplying 3 out, an endless sequence spaced 3 apart. The factors of a number are finite; its multiples never stop. Pick any divisor column and read its multiples on the

items.page: GCD: Greatest Common Divisor & Euclidean Algorithm
items.caption: Coprime without being prime
items.text: The factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8; the factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5, 15. The only chip the two rows share is 1, so gcd(8, 15) = 1 and the numbers are coprime. Neither 8 nor 15 is prime: coprimality is about the pair having no common factor, not about either number on its own.

items.secTitle: When aaa and bbb Are Coprime
items.caption: Coprime numbers meet only at their product
items.text: The multiples of 7 and the multiples of 9 run side by side from 0 to 63. Because 7 and 9 share no factor except 1, no multiple of 7 below 63 is also a multiple of 9: the two tracks first line up at 63 = 7 · 9. For coprime numbers the LCM is the full product.

items.caption: Three fifths as parts of a bar
items.text: The bar is one whole. The denominator 5 cuts it into five equal parts, so each part is one fifth. The numerator 3 counts how many of those parts are taken: the three shaded cells. Together they describe 3/5, three parts of size 1/5.

items.caption: Proper and improper on the same whole
items.text: Both bars use the same length for one whole. 3/4 shades three of four quarters and stays inside a single bar: a proper fraction, less than 1. 5/3 needs five thirds, but one bar holds only three, so the shading fills a whole bar and two thirds of a second one: an improper fraction, 5/3 = 1 2/3, greater than 1.

items.caption: Unit fractions shrink as the denominator grows
items.text: Each bar is the same whole with exactly one part shaded. Cutting into 2, then 4, then 8 equal parts halves the part each time, so 1/2 > 1/4 > 1/8. A larger denominator means more, and therefore smaller, pieces.

items.caption: Adding sevenths
items.text: All three bars are cut into sevenths, so every part has the same size. Two parts and three more parts make five parts: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. The denominator names the size of the parts and does not change; only the number of parts is added.

items.caption: Adding 2/3 and 1/4 through twelfths
items.text: Thirds and quarters are different sizes, so 2/3 and 1/4 cannot be added part by part. Cutting both bars into twelfths, the least common denominator, turns 2/3 into 8/12 and 1/4 into 3/12. Now the parts match and the counts add: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12, shown on the last bar.

items.caption: Why 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5
items.text: Adding tops and bottoms gives 2/5, but the 2/5 bar is shorter than the 1/2 bar on its own, and adding a positive amount cannot make something smaller. Converting to sixths gives the true sum: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, the amber bar.

items.caption: Three quarters against three sevenths
items.text: Both bars are the same whole and both take 3 parts. The top bar is cut into 4 parts, the bottom into 7, so each seventh is smaller than each quarter. Three larger parts cover more of the bar: 3/4 > 3/7.

items.caption: Comparing 3/4 and 5/6 in twelfths
items.text: 3/4 and 5/6 cut the whole differently, so their parts cannot be counted against each other. In twelfths, the least common denominator of 4 and 6, 3/4 becomes 9/12 and 5/6 becomes 10/12. Now the parts are the same size and the counts decide: 10 > 9, so 5/6 is larger, by exactly one twelfth.

items.caption: Using 1/2 as a benchmark
items.text: On the line from 0 to 1, the dashed mark is 1/2. Three eighths is less than four eighths, so 3/8 lies left of it; five ninths is more than four and a half ninths, so 5/9 lies right of it. A fraction on each side of the benchmark settles the comparison without any common denominator: 5/9 > 3/8.

items.caption: What 1/2 over 3/4 measures
items.text: The complex fraction (1/2)/(3/4) asks what part of 3/4 the amount 1/2 is. In quarters, 3/4 is 3 parts and 1/2 is 2 parts of the same size, so 1/2 is 2 of the 3 parts: 2/3. Multiplying top and bottom by the LCD 4 does the same thing in one step: (1/2 · 4)/(3/4 · 4) = 2/3.

items.caption: How many quarters fit in a half
items.text: 1/2 ÷ 1/4 asks how many quarters fit into one half. On bars of the same whole, the half covers exactly the same length as two quarters, so the answer is 2. Multiplying by the reciprocal gives the same count: 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2.

items.caption: Three quarters divided by 2

items.caption: Equivalent fractions share one point
items.text: The interval from 0 to 1 is marked in halves, quarters and sixths. On each line the filled point is half-way: 1/2, 2/4 and 3/6. The dashed line shows that all three are the same point; only the spacing of the marks around it differs.

items.secTitle: Converting Improper Fractions to Mixed Numbers
items.caption: Seventeen fifths as a mixed number
items.text: Seventeen parts of size 1/5 are laid out on bars of five fifths each. Three bars fill completely, using 15 fifths, and 2 fifths are left over on a fourth bar. That is the division 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2: the quotient counts the full wholes, the remainder the leftover parts, so 17/5 = 3 2/5.

items.secTitle: Mixed Numbers on the Number Line
items.caption: 2 2/5 on the number line
items.text: Each whole from 0 to 3 is cut into fifths. Counting two whole steps and then two more fifths lands on the amber point, 2 2/5. Counting fifths from 0 instead takes 12 steps to the same point, so 2 2/5 and 12/5 are two names for one number, lying two fifths of the way from 2 to 3.

items.caption: Two thirds of four fifths
items.text: The unit square is cut into 3 columns and 5 rows, 15 equal cells. Two of the three columns are 2/3 of the square; four of the five rows are 4/5 of it. The cells in both, amber, are 2/3 of 4/5: 2 · 4 = 8 of the 3 · 5 = 15 cells. That is why the numerators multiply and the denominators multiply: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15.

items.caption: Four times two thirds
items.text: 4 × 2/3 is four copies of 2/3. Each copy shades 2 thirds, so together they shade 8 thirds. Eight thirds fill two whole bars and two thirds of a third bar: 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3. The whole number multiplies the numerator; the size of the parts, the denominator, stays the same.

items.caption: Six slots, six possible remainders: 0 to 5
items.text: The wheel has exactly six slots and every integer lands in one of them, so there are exactly six possible remainders mod 6, from 0 to 5, and none can equal 6 itself: that would be slot 0 again. The slots are the complete set of residues. Change the modulus and count the slots on the

items.caption: Finding 47 mod 5 on a number line
items.text: Jumps of 5 from 0 land on 5, 10, 15, …, 45. A tenth jump would reach 50, past 47, so only 9 jumps fit: that is the integer part of 47 ÷ 5 = 9.4. The nearest multiple of 5 at or below 47 is 9 · 5 = 45, and the gap from 45 to 47 is the remainder: 47 mod 5 = 2.

items.page: Modulo of Negative Numbers: Truncated vs Floored Division
items.caption: Two ways to divide −7 by 3
items.text: The circles mark the multiples of 3 and the amber dot is −7. Truncated division rounds −7 ÷ 3 = −2.33 toward zero, to q = −2, and uses the multiple −6 to the right of −7: the remainder is −7 − (−6) = −1. Floored division rounds down, to q = −3, and uses the multiple −9 to the left: the remainder is −7 − (−9) = 2. Both satisfy −7 = 3q + r.

items.page: Modulo of Negative Numbers: Truncated vs Floored Division
items.caption: One class, many representatives
items.text: Every number in a slot is congruent to every other: −1 and 2 occupy the same slot mod 3 just as 3, 9 and 15 share a slot mod 6 here, so the two conventions’ answers, −1 and 2, are two names for one class. items.page: Modular Arithmetic: Operations, Power Cycles & Applications
items.caption: The powers of 2 modulo 7 repeat
items.text: Each dot is 2ᵏ mod 7 for k = 1 to 9. The values run 2, 4, 1 and then start over, because 2³ = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7) and multiplying by 2 again returns to 2. The amber dots mark where each new cycle begins, at k = 1, 4, 7. Any exponent can be reduced by the cycle length 3: 100 = 3 · 33 + 1, so 2¹⁰⁰ mod 7 equals 2¹ mod 7 = 2.

items.caption: The distributive property as an array
items.text: Three rows of nine dots make 3 · 9 = 3 · (4 + 5) = 27. A line after the fourth column splits every row into 4 blue dots and 5 amber dots. Counting the parts separately gives 3 · 4 = 12 blue and 3 · 5 = 15 amber, and 12 + 15 = 27: the same dots counted two ways, which is exactly 3(4 + 5) = 3 · 4 + 3 · 5.

items.text: Green 3 and its multiples from 9 up. Numbers divisible by both 2 and 3 — 12, 18, 24 and their kin — now wear both colors striped.

items.caption: mod 6, zero class pinned, frozen
items.text: The gold-edged slice holds 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 — the multiples of 6, the only class where divisibility is true.
